transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Doctor... honestly, I don't even know where to begin, because it's like I'm not even the same person I used to be. It's just this heavy, empty feeling, you know? Like... mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore. I used to be so active. I was a protective service worker, always on the go, always alert. I had my bachelor's degree, I had plans, I had things I loved. I used to go hiking up in the mountains every single weekend, rain or shine. I loved the fresh air, the physical exertion, just being out there in nature. And I coached a little league team, too—loved those kids, loved teaching them the game. I even played guitar. I'd sit on my porch for hours just strumming and singing, learning new songs. But now? Now I've stopped all of it. I don't hike. I haven't picked up my guitar in months, it's just gathering dust in the corner. I don't coach anymore. I don't even call people back. My phone will ring and I'll just stare at it, watching the name flash on the screen, and I just can't bring myself to answer or even send a text. And some days... some days are the worst. I just sit in that small rental house I have, just sitting in a chair or on the edge of the bed for hours. Just staring at the wall. And the thing is, I know there are things I need to do. I know there are dishes in the sink, or bills to pay, or even just taking a shower, but I just... I can't make myself start. It's like the starter motor in my brain is completely broken and I'm just stuck there, paralyzed, while the hours just tick by. It's just so exhausting doing absolutely nothing.
When did this heavy, empty feeling and loss of interest in activities first start? Was there a specific time or event, or did it come on gradually?

Well, it wasn't exactly like a light switch, you know? It wasn't just one morning I woke up and everything was suddenly gray and heavy. It was more like... well, things really started unraveling, just completely coming apart at the seams, right around the time I moved into that smaller rental house. That was... let's see, it's been about a year and two months ago now. Yeah, roughly fourteen months. 

Because that was right after the divorce was finalized. And you know, going through a divorce, it just takes so much out of you—the paperwork, the lawyers, the dividing up of a life you built for years. We used to have a bigger place, a nice yard, a garage where I kept all my hiking gear and my tools, and then suddenly I'm boxing up my half of a life and dragging it into this tiny, cramped rental across town. I remember the first night there, just looking at all the cardboard boxes stacked up in the living room, and I told myself I would unpack them the next weekend. I had a whole plan. But the weekend came and went, and I just... I didn't. I couldn't. 

It's like the energy just started leaking out of me right then, a year and two months ago. At first, I told myself I was just exhausted from the move, from the emotional toll of the divorce, because you know how people say you just need time to adjust to a new normal? They tell you to give it time. But the new normal just kept getting heavier and heavier. I'd sit on the couch—well, it wasn't even my good couch, she kept that one, I just had this old hand-me-down—and I'd just watch the dust motes floating in the air from the window. I'd watch the sun move across the floor and realize the whole day was gone. So yeah, about a year and two months. That's when the thread got pulled and my whole life just started unraveling on me.

You mentioned the heavy feeling started around the time of the move and divorce about 14 months ago. But I want to be clear: did your mood and loss of interest start right around that same time, or did they develop gradually over the weeks and months after you moved into the rental house?

Well, it's... it's a little hard to untangle exactly. Because, like I said, when I first got to that rental house, I just thought I was tired. I really did. I thought, 'Okay, I've just been through the wringer, I'm emotionally drained, I just need a minute to catch my breath.' So those first few weeks, maybe even the first month or two, I'd tell myself that I was just taking a break from hiking, you know? Just resting my legs. Or I'd look at the guitar and think, 'My calluses are peeling, I'll pick it up next week when my head is clearer.' 

But then... the weeks just kept rolling by. I remember it was around Thanksgiving, so maybe a few months after the move, and my buddy called me to go do this trail up by the ridge that we always used to do every autumn because the leaves are just incredible up there. And I remember holding the phone, and I just... I didn't even want to go. It wasn't just that I was tired anymore; I literally felt nothing at the thought of it. No excitement, no desire to see the leaves, just... blankness. 

So I guess it was gradual. It crept up on me. At first, it was just the boxes not getting unpacked, and then it was the dishes piling up, and then it was ignoring phone calls, and before I knew it, I was just sitting in that chair all day. It didn't all hit me the very first day I walked into the house, it just sort of... seeped in, like water in a basement, until suddenly I realized I was drowning in it and I didn't even care about the things I used to love. It just faded out, slowly, over those first few months until there was nothing left but this heavy, stuck feeling.

Before this past year and two months—before the divorce and the move—have you ever experienced a period like this before, where you felt this heavy, empty feeling and lost interest in things you normally enjoyed, lasting for weeks or more?

Well, let me think back... before the divorce, before everything got packed up and moved... no, not like this. I mean, sure, everyone has bad days, right? You have a tough week at work—and in protective services, believe me, you have some really tough weeks, you see things that just weigh on you, you know? And sometimes I'd come home after a long shift and I just wouldn't want to talk to anybody, I'd just want to sit on the porch with a beer and zone out for an evening. But that was just being tired. That was just needing to decompress. I'd wake up the next morning, or at least by Saturday, and I'd be ready to go. I'd be packing my gear, checking the weather report, texting the guys to see who was up for a hike. 

I never had anything like this... this absolute emptiness. This feeling where even the thought of doing something I love just feels like trying to move a boulder uphill. It's completely new. Before all this started fourteen months ago, I was always the guy organizing things. I was the one saying, 'Hey, let's get the team together for extra batting practice,' or 'Let's try that new trail up past the old fire tower.' I was always moving. So no, I've never had a time where I just shut down like this for weeks on end. It's like I was driving a car at sixty miles an hour my whole life, and then suddenly the engine just dropped out right onto the highway, and I've just been sitting on the shoulder ever since, watching the traffic go by, not even caring that I'm stranded. So, no, nothing like this before. Never.

I want to make sure I have the full picture. Before this past 14 months, have you ever had a period—even a shorter one, maybe just a few weeks—where you felt depressed, down, or lost interest in things, even if it wasn't as severe as what you're experiencing now?

Well, let me really rack my brain here, because I want to be absolutely sure I'm giving you the right picture. But... no. Honestly, no. I mean, even if we go way back, right? Back to when I was getting my bachelor's degree, pulling those crazy all-nighters, or when I first joined the service. I mean, the training academy was brutal, they push you to your absolute physical and mental limits just to see if you'll break under the pressure. And yeah, it was incredibly stressful. Or, you know, when I had my first real bad breakup in my twenties... I never got down like this. Not like a cloud hanging over me for weeks where I didn't care about anything. 

I'd be upset for a couple of days, sure. Maybe I'd be in a foul mood and just go hit the heavy bag at the gym until my knuckles were raw, but I never lost interest in the gym itself, you see what I mean? I always had this... this motor running inside me. If I had a bad week or a really rough case at work, I'd cope by doing more, not less. I'd pick up an extra shift, or I'd go out and chop wood for the fire pit, or I'd tear apart a carburetor in the garage just to keep my hands busy and my mind occupied. I never had a time, not even for a week or two, where I just didn't care about my projects or my hobbies. 

It's just so completely foreign to who I am... or who I was, anyway. I was always the guy who bounced back. It's like I lived my whole life up until a year ago as this one, high-energy, get-things-done kind of person, and then the divorce happened, that move happened, and I just... morphed into someone else entirely. Someone who just sits and stares at the wall and can't even be bothered to open the mail. So to answer your question, no, not even a mild version of this. Not even for a week. This is all completely new, and honestly, it's just bizarre because I don't even recognize the guy in the mirror anymore. But before fourteen months ago? Never.

Have you ever had periods where you felt the opposite—like you had tons of energy, maybe even more than usual, where you needed less sleep than normal, or your thoughts were racing, or you felt unusually confident or on top of the world?

The opposite? Like... feeling on top of the world, bouncing off the walls? No. No, definitely not. I mean, like I was saying before, I always had a good motor, I liked to stay busy, but not in a... not in an out-of-control way. Not like what you're describing. 

Take the sleep thing, for example. I've always needed my sleep. In protective services, you absolutely have to be sharp. It's not a job where you can just skate by on a couple of hours of rest. If you're running on two hours of sleep, your reaction time drops, your situational awareness goes out the window, and suddenly you're a liability to yourself and your team. So, no, I never had a time where I just didn't need to sleep. I've always been an eight-hours-a-night kind of guy. Well, maybe seven if the alarm goes off early for a fishing trip, or if I wanted to get the boat out on the water before the sun came up, but you know what I mean. I always crashed eventually.

And as far as thoughts racing... no, my thoughts were always pretty organized. They had to be. You have to be organized when you're managing a chaotic scene, right? You have to look at the variables, secure the area, figure out who needs what, communicate with dispatch. If your mind is just bouncing all over the place like a pinball, you can't do the job. I was confident, sure. I knew what I was doing. When you've got your degree and you've been on the job for years, you build up a certain level of, I guess, professional authority. You walk into a room and you know how to handle the situation, you know how to talk people down. But it wasn't like... like I thought I was Superman or invincible or anything crazy like that. It was just competence. 

I remember back in, oh, it must have been 2018 or 2019, we had this massive storm system roll through. It knocked out power for half the county, trees down everywhere, total gridlock. I worked maybe sixty or seventy hours in four days. I was running on black coffee and pure adrenaline, and yeah, I was moving fast, getting things done, directing crews, pulling debris off the roads. But even then, even with all that adrenaline pumping, when my shift finally ended, I was dead on my feet. I went home, peeled my boots off, and I think I slept for fourteen hours straight. I didn't stay up remodeling the kitchen or whatever it is people do when they're wired. 

So, no. I've never had a period where my brain was just stuck in overdrive for no reason, or where I felt like I didn't need to rest. I was just a normal, active guy who liked to stay busy and get things done. Never anything extreme like what you're asking about. Just steady. Until, you know, this past year when the bottom just fell out completely.

During those 14 months since the move, or even before that, have you ever had a stretch of time where you felt unusually energized, optimistic, or like you were taking on too many projects at once—even if it only lasted a few days or a week?

No, no, definitely not. I mean, especially not in these past fourteen months. Since the divorce and the move... man, there hasn't been a single day of feeling energized or optimistic. I remember when I was actually doing the move, right? I rented this big twenty-foot box truck, and I was loading it up mostly by myself because I didn't want to drag the guys from work into my mess on their weekend off. And I remember just staring at the boxes, feeling like they weighed a thousand pounds each. There was absolutely no energy there, no optimism about a fresh start or anything like that. It took everything I had just to tape the boxes shut and push them up the ramp. 

And as for taking on too many projects... that’s just never been my style, even before all this happened. I’m a very methodical guy. You have to be in my line of work. If you try to juggle too many things at once on a scene, you get sloppy. You miss a detail on an incident report, or you overlook a safety hazard, and somebody gets hurt. So I’ve always been a 'one thing at a time' kind of person. If I’m fixing the lawnmower on a Saturday, I’m just fixing the lawnmower. I don’t pull the spark plugs out and then suddenly decide I need to go paint the garage and reorganize the attic at the same time. That’s just not how my brain works. I like to finish what I start, sweep up the sawdust, put the tools back on the pegboard exactly where they belong, and then maybe think about the next thing. 

So, no, I’ve never had a week or even a couple of days where I felt like I was taking on the world or juggling a dozen things. And like I said, since the move, it’s just been a complete flatline. No spikes of energy, no sudden bursts of optimism, no urges to start a new hobby or build a deck. Just... sitting around, feeling heavy, completely drained. So no, nothing like what you're talking about.

I want to make sure I haven't missed anything. Even if it was just for a few days in a row, have you ever had a time where you felt really good, like things were going great, and you were accomplishing a lot of things—maybe working on multiple projects at once, or feeling like you didn't need much sleep because you were too excited or motivated to rest?

I know you're just being thorough, Doc, and I appreciate it, I really do, because a lot of guys in my line of work, they go to a doctor and the doctor just rushes them out the door in five minutes with a prescription and a pat on the back. But I gotta tell you, it's just like I was saying a minute ago. No. Never. 

I’ve had good days, sure. I mean, obviously, right? Let’s go back to... man, maybe 2012? I got commended for how I handled a multi-vehicle pileup out on the interstate. It was an absolute mess—freezing rain, cars scattered everywhere, people panicking. I managed the scene, kept everyone calm, got the EMTs in and out safely. Afterwards, the captain actually pulled me aside and said I did a hell of a job. And yeah, I felt good. I felt proud. I went home and I told my ex-wife about it, and we ordered a pizza from that place down on 4th street—the one that closed a few years ago, which is a shame, they had the best deep dish in the city—and we celebrated. 

But I didn't stay up all night. I didn't suddenly decide to rebuild the transmission in my truck or start painting the living room because I was so pumped up. I ate my pizza, I watched a little TV, and I went to bed at my normal time, because I had to be up at 0500 the next day and I knew it. I've always been grounded like that. If things were going great, I just enjoyed the moment, you know? I never got this... this euphoric, electrified feeling you're talking about. 

Even when we bought our first house, or when I finally finished my bachelor's degree—which took me six years, by the way, taking night classes while working full shifts, which was just an absolute grind and a half. When they finally handed me that diploma, I was thrilled. But I was also exhausted. I celebrated by sleeping in on a Sunday and doing absolutely nothing. So, this idea of being so excited I don't need sleep, or doing a million things at once... it's just not me. It's never been me. I don't know how else to explain it, but I've always just been a steady-as-she-goes kind of guy. I never had these extreme highs. Just a normal, level baseline... until everything just completely dropped off a cliff this past year.
During these past 14 months when you've been feeling this heavy, empty way and sitting in that chair staring at the wall, have you ever had thoughts about harming yourself or wishing you were dead?

No. No, I haven't. I know it probably sounds like I would, given how I’ve just been describing everything, just sitting there for hours on end, but... no. It’s not like that. 

I mean, I’ve seen that firsthand, right? In my line of work, you get called out to those scenes. I remember this one call, back in maybe 2015, out on the east side of town. A guy had lost his job, going through a rough patch, and he just... well, he took his own life out in his garage. And I had to be the one to secure the scene and wait for the coroner, and I was there when his brother showed up, just completely, utterly broken. You see something like that, the absolute devastation it leaves behind for the people who are still here, and it sticks with you. It really does. It gets under your skin. You never forget the sound a person makes when they get that kind of news. 

So even now, with the divorce, and living in this new place—which, by the way, is just this cramped little apartment that always smells faintly like boiled cabbage no matter how much I open the windows or scrub the floors—even with all of that, and feeling as low as a guy can possibly feel, my brain just doesn't go there. 

When I’m sitting in that chair... it’s this old brown hand-me-down recliner I picked up, the mechanism is half broken so it doesn't even lean back right, but it's where I end up... when I'm just sitting there staring at the drywall, I’m not plotting anything. I’m not wishing I was dead. It’s more like... I just don't have the energy to participate in being alive, if that makes any sense? It's not wanting to die, it's just feeling like the battery is completely drained to zero and the alternator is shot and there's no way to recharge it. It's just a heavy, blank feeling. But taking myself out? Harming myself? No, Doc. I've never had thoughts like that. Never.
During these past 14 months, have you noticed any changes in your appetite or your weight—either eating more or less than you normally do, or gaining or losing weight without trying?

Appetite... weight... no, I can't say that I have. No changes there. 

I mean, I know a lot of guys, when they go through the wringer—a divorce, a move, all that stress—they either hit the bottle and blow up like a balloon, or they just stop eating entirely and waste away to nothing. You see it all the time in my line of work. The stress eats at them. But for me... no. My weight has been sitting at a solid 190 pounds since I was about twenty-eight years old, and it hasn't budged an inch, even these past fourteen months. 

I know this for a fact because I wear the exact same size uniform pants I've worn for the last decade. You know the ones—those heavy navy-blue poly-blend trousers with the reinforced knees? The department issues us three new pairs a year, and I always just check the exact same boxes on the quartermaster's requisition form: 34 waist, 32 inseam. They still fit exactly the same. Even my duty belt still fastens on the exact same notch—the third hole from the end. It’s actually got a little wear mark right on that spot from where the brass buckle rubs against the leather every single shift for years. If I was gaining or losing weight, that belt would be the first thing to tell me, because you feel it immediately when you're carrying all that gear around your waist. 

And as for my appetite... it's just the same as it's always been, which is to say, I eat because I have to. It’s exactly like putting gas in the truck. I don't really get cravings for anything, but I haven't stopped eating, either. It’s just... routine. Every Sunday, even now, even when I'm feeling like I'm dragging a hundred-pound anchor around and I can barely get out of that broken recliner I told you about, I force myself to go to the grocery store over on 5th Avenue. The one with the terrible parking lot where people just leave their carts right in the middle of the empty spaces. 

I go in, I buy the exact same things: a loaf of wheat bread, a pound of sliced turkey breast, some apples, a bag of coffee, and those pre-made salads in the plastic clamshells. I come home, I put them in the fridge. And then during the week, I just eat them. I don't really even taste it anymore, to be perfectly honest with you. It's just fuel. I sit in the chair, I eat my turkey sandwich, I throw the paper plate in the trash, and that's it. I'm definitely not eating more, because I don't get any joy out of food right now, no urges to go grab a burger or order a pizza like I used to. And I'm not eating less, because I know if I skip meals, I'll get lightheaded on the job, and I absolutely cannot have that. My squad relies on me to be alert. 

So, no. No changes in the weight, no changes in how much I eat. It's just the exact same maintenance routine, week in and week out, just keeping the engine running even though the car isn't really going anywhere.
During these past 14 months, have you noticed any changes in your sleep? For example, are you sleeping more than you normally do, or having trouble falling asleep or staying asleep at night?

Sleep? No. No, honestly, sleep is about the only thing in my life that hasn't completely flipped upside down on me. 

I mean, you’d think I’d be tossing and turning, right? With everything that’s happened—the divorce, the move to this tiny place, just feeling like I'm dragging that anchor around all day—most guys I know would be up all night staring at the ceiling fan. My ex-wife, actually, she had terrible insomnia whenever she got stressed. She used to get up and pace the hardwood floors in our old house, make this chamomile tea that smelled like wet weeds, and just wander around. Drove me crazy because the floorboards right outside our bedroom door had this awful squeak, and you could hear it all the way down the hall. 

But me? I've never been like that. Even now. I go to bed at 2100 hours, maybe 2130 at the absolute latest, because like I told you, I have to be up at 0500 for my shift. It’s a discipline thing. I bought this cheap, firm mattress from a discount place out on Highway 9 when I first moved into this apartment—the guy tied it to the roof of my truck with twine, if you can believe that, I had to drive twenty miles an hour all the way home—and the second my head hits the pillow, I'm out. Takes me maybe ten minutes to fall asleep. 

And I stay asleep, too. The walls in this complex are paper thin. The people upstairs have this dog, sounds like a beagle mix maybe, that howls, and sometimes it sounds like they’re dropping bowling balls on the floor at two in the morning. But it doesn't wake me up. I sleep right through it, solid as a rock, same as I always have. 

And as for sleeping more... no, I don't do that either. You'd think, given how drained I feel, how I just don't have the energy to participate in anything, that I'd just stay in bed for fourteen hours a day. But my body just doesn't work like that. My eyes snap open at 0455, exactly five minutes before my alarm goes off. It’s this old digital clock I've had since my night-class days, with these glaring red LED numbers that are almost too bright for the room. But I always beat it by five minutes. Even on my days off, I’m awake at 0455. I just get up, make my coffee, and move over to that broken brown recliner. I don't go back to sleep. So, no... falling asleep, staying asleep, how much I sleep... it's all exactly the same routine it's been for the last twenty years. No changes there at all.

During these past 14 months, have you found yourself feeling guilty about the divorce, or blaming yourself for how things turned out? Or do you feel like you're worthless or that you've let people down?

Guilty? Worthless? No. No, I wouldn't say that at all. 

I mean, look, the divorce... it was just a thing that happened. It’s like a contract expiring. We were married, and then we just weren't anymore. I remember the exact day we went to the mediator to finalize the division of assets. It was this stuffy little office downtown, right across the street from the municipal courthouse where I have to go testify on cases sometimes. The air conditioning in this guy's office was completely busted, and he just kept wiping his forehead with this yellow handkerchief the whole time we were talking. We sat there, and we divided up the furniture, the savings accounts... I didn't fight her on any of it. She wanted the house, fine. She wanted the good pots and pans, the television, fine. I just packed my duffel bags, grabbed my uniforms, and moved into that cramped apartment I told you about.

But feeling guilty about it? Blaming myself? No. It takes two people to build a marriage, and it takes two people to let it fall apart. We just stopped connecting. The shifts I work—rotating days, nights, weekends, the mandatory overtime—it just grinds you down. You come home and you just want absolute quiet. She wanted to go out, she wanted to talk, and I just... I didn't have the words. But that's just the reality of the job. You ask any guy in my unit, they'll tell you the divorce rate in our line of work is astronomical. It's just a statistic. I don't feel like I failed or let her down. I provided for her, I paid the mortgage on time every single month, I never missed a payment or did her wrong.

And as for feeling worthless... no, I don't get that either. I know exactly what I'm worth. I put on my uniform, I do my job, I keep people safe. I've got a bachelor's degree in criminal justice, I've got commendations in my personnel file. I know I have value. It's just... like I was saying before about the recliner, I just feel heavy and empty. The battery is dead. But I don't sit there beating myself up or thinking I'm a bad person. It's not a pity party. It's just... a blank slate. So, no, no guilt. No feeling worthless. It just is what it is.

I want to go back and ask you one more time to be absolutely certain: Looking at your entire life before that move 14 months ago—your childhood, your teenage years, your twenties, your thirties—was there ever even a two-week stretch where you felt down, blue, or sad, or where you lost interest in things you normally cared about?

Before the move? No. I can say with absolute certainty, no. 

I mean, you're asking about my whole life, so let's just look at it. Childhood, teenage years... I was always an even-keeled kid. I grew up over in the north end of town, normal house, normal parents. I played baseball—catcher, mostly, because I liked being involved in every single pitch, calling the game from behind the plate. I had this heavy Rawlings leather mitt that I oiled every single Sunday night with this special conditioner my dad bought at the hardware store. I never sat around moping or feeling blue. I wasn't one of those brooding teenagers who locked themselves in their room to listen to sad music. I was just focused. I knew early on I wanted to get into the department, so I kept my nose clean, did the work, and got my bachelor's degree in criminal justice at the state college. 

Then my twenties... well, my twenties were the academy and my rookie years. You don't have time to feel sad in the academy. They run you absolutely ragged. I remember my training officer, Sergeant Miller—this guy had a voice like a gravel crusher, used to make us run the perimeter track at 0400 in the freezing rain if even one guy's boots weren't shined to a mirror finish. But I didn't lose interest in it. I didn't get down about it. I thrived on it. I loved the structure. I was always the first one on the line, ready to go. 

And my thirties? Same thing. Just working the beat, putting my time in, moving up to senior patrol. I was always the guy who took the extra shifts. If someone called out sick on the swing shift, dispatch knew they could call me. I'd put the uniform on, lace up my boots—those heavy black leather tactical boots with the side-zips, you know, they take about a month of solid walking to break in properly, but once you do they fit like a glove—and I'd just go out there and do the job. I liked my life. I liked my routine. I liked going to the firing range on my days off to keep my qualification scores up, I liked grilling on the back patio at the old house with my ex-wife before things got quiet between us. I cared about all of it. 

So, no. Never. There was never a two-week stretch, or even a two-day stretch, where I felt down or blue or lost interest in the things I cared about. My baseline was always just... steady. A perfectly straight line. I was reliable. It wasn't until fourteen months ago, when I packed those duffel bags and ended up in this tiny apartment, sitting in that broken brown recliner, that the battery just completely died on me and this heavy feeling set in. But before that? Not once. Not ever.

Well, it wasn't exactly like a light switch, you know? It wasn't just one morning I woke up and everything was suddenly gray and heavy. That was... let's see, it's been about a year and two months ago now. Yeah, roughly fourteen months. 

Because that was right after the divorce was finalized. And you know, going through a divorce, it just takes so much out of you—the paperwork, the lawyers, the dividing up of a life you built for years. We used to have a bigger place, a nice yard, a garage where I kept all my hiking gear and my tools, and then suddenly I'm boxing up my half of a life and dragging it into this tiny, cramped rental across town. They tell you to give it time. But the new normal just kept getting heavier and heavier. patient.answer:
Well, it's... it's a little hard to untangle exactly. Because, like I said, when I first got to that rental house, I just thought I was tired. I really did. I remember it was around Thanksgiving, so maybe a few months after the move, and my buddy called me to go do this trail up by the ridge that we always used to do every autumn because the leaves are just incredible up there. It didn't all hit me the very first day I walked into the house, it just sort of... seeped in, like water in a basement, until suddenly I realized I was drowning in it and I didn't even care about the things I used to love. patient.answer:
The opposite? Like... feeling on top of the world, bouncing off the walls? No. No, definitely not. I mean, like I was saying before, I always had a good motor, I liked to stay busy, but not in a... not in an out-of-control way. Not like what you're describing. 

Take the sleep thing, for example. I've always needed my sleep. In protective services, you absolutely have to be sharp. It's not a job where you can just skate by on a couple of hours of rest. If you're running on two hours of sleep, your reaction time drops, your situational awareness goes out the window, and suddenly you're a liability to yourself and your team. So, no, I never had a time where I just didn't need to sleep. I've always been an eight-hours-a-night kind of guy. Well, maybe seven if the alarm goes off early for a fishing trip, or if I wanted to get the boat out on the water before the sun came up, but you know what I mean. I always crashed eventually.

And as far as thoughts racing... no, my thoughts were always pretty organized. They had to be. You have to be organized when you're managing a chaotic scene, right? You have to look at the variables, secure the area, figure out who needs what, communicate with dispatch. If your mind is just bouncing all over the place like a pinball, you can't do the job. I was confident, sure. I knew what I was doing. When you've got your degree and you've been on the job for years, you build up a certain level of, I guess, professional authority. You walk into a room and you know how to handle the situation, you know how to talk people down. But it wasn't like... like I thought I was Superman or invincible or anything crazy like that. It was just competence. 

I remember back in, oh, it must have been 2018 or 2019, we had this massive storm system roll through. It knocked out power for half the county, trees down everywhere, total gridlock. I worked maybe sixty or seventy hours in four days. I was running on black coffee and pure adrenaline, and yeah, I was moving fast, getting things done, directing crews, pulling debris off the roads. But even then, even with all that adrenaline pumping, when my shift finally ended, I was dead on my feet. I went home, peeled my boots off, and I think I slept for fourteen hours straight. I didn't stay up remodeling the kitchen or whatever it is people do when they're wired. 

So, no. I've never had a period where my brain was just stuck in overdrive for no reason, or where I felt like I didn't need to rest. I was just a normal, active guy who liked to stay busy and get things done. Never anything extreme like what you're asking about. Just steady. Until, you know, this past year when the bottom just fell out completely.

And I remember just staring at the boxes, feeling like they weighed a thousand pounds each. There was absolutely no energy there, no optimism about a fresh start or anything like that. It took everything I had just to tape the boxes shut and push them up the ramp. 

And as for taking on too many projects... that’s just never been my style, even before all this happened. I’m a very methodical guy. You have to be in my line of work. So I’ve always been a 'one thing at a time' kind of person. If I’m fixing the lawnmower on a Saturday, I’m just fixing the lawnmower. I don’t pull the spark plugs out and then suddenly decide I need to go paint the garage and reorganize the attic at the same time. That’s just not how my brain works. I like to finish what I start, sweep up the sawdust, put the tools back on the pegboard exactly where they belong, and then maybe think about the next thing. 

So, no, I’ve never had a week or even a couple of days where I felt like I was taking on the world or juggling a dozen things. And like I said, since the move, it’s just been a complete flatline. No spikes of energy, no sudden bursts of optimism, no urges to start a new hobby or build a deck. Just... sitting around, feeling heavy, completely drained. patient.answer:
I know you're just being thorough, Doc, and I appreciate it, I really do, because a lot of guys in my line of work, they go to a doctor and the doctor just rushes them out the door in five minutes with a prescription and a pat on the back. But I gotta tell you, it's just like I was saying a minute ago. No. Never. 

I’ve had good days, sure. I mean, obviously, right? Let’s go back to... man, maybe 2012? I got commended for how I handled a multi-vehicle pileup out on the interstate. It was an absolute mess—freezing rain, cars scattered everywhere, people panicking. I managed the scene, kept everyone calm, got the EMTs in and out safely. Afterwards, the captain actually pulled me aside and said I did a hell of a job. And yeah, I felt good. I felt proud. I went home and I told my ex-wife about it, and we ordered a pizza from that place down on 4th street—the one that closed a few years ago, which is a shame, they had the best deep dish in the city—and we celebrated. 

But I didn't stay up all night. I didn't suddenly decide to rebuild the transmission in my truck or start painting the living room because I was so pumped up. I ate my pizza, I watched a little TV, and I went to bed at my normal time, because I had to be up at 0500 the next day and I knew it. I've always been grounded like that. If things were going great, I just enjoyed the moment, you know? I never got this... this euphoric, electrified feeling you're talking about. 

Even when we bought our first house, or when I finally finished my bachelor's degree—which took me six years, by the way, taking night classes while working full shifts, which was just an absolute grind and a half. When they finally handed me that diploma, I was thrilled. But I was also exhausted. I celebrated by sleeping in on a Sunday and doing absolutely nothing. So, this idea of being so excited I don't need sleep, or doing a million things at once... it's just not me. It's never been me. I don't know how else to explain it, but I've always just been a steady-as-she-goes kind of guy. I never had these extreme highs. Just a normal, level baseline... until everything just completely dropped off a cliff this past year.

patient.answer:
No. No, I haven't. I know it probably sounds like I would, given how I’ve just been describing everything, just sitting there for hours on end, but... no. It’s not like that. 

I mean, I’ve seen that firsthand, right? In my line of work, you get called out to those scenes. I remember this one call, back in maybe 2015, out on the east side of town. A guy had lost his job, going through a rough patch, and he just... well, he took his own life out in his garage. And I had to be the one to secure the scene and wait for the coroner, and I was there when his brother showed up, just completely, utterly broken. You see something like that, the absolute devastation it leaves behind for the people who are still here, and it sticks with you. It really does. It gets under your skin. You never forget the sound a person makes when they get that kind of news. 

So even now, with the divorce, and living in this new place—which, by the way, is just this cramped little apartment that always smells faintly like boiled cabbage no matter how much I open the windows or scrub the floors—even with all of that, and feeling as low as a guy can possibly feel, my brain just doesn't go there. 

When I’m sitting in that chair... it’s this old brown hand-me-down recliner I picked up, the mechanism is half broken so it doesn't even lean back right, but it's where I end up... when I'm just sitting there staring at the drywall, I’m not plotting anything. I’m not wishing I was dead. It’s more like... I just don't have the energy to participate in being alive, if that makes any sense? It's not wanting to die, it's just feeling like the battery is completely drained to zero and the alternator is shot and there's no way to recharge it. It's just a heavy, blank feeling. But taking myself out? Harming myself? No, Doc. I've never had thoughts like that. Never.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has experienced significant changes in appetite, weight, or sleep patterns during these 14 months of depression, which would help confirm the diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder and rule out adjustment disorder or other conditions.
doctor.question: During these past 14 months, have you noticed any changes in your appetite or your weight—either eating more or less than you normally do, or gaining or losing weight without trying?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in appetite or weight, which are symptoms of depression or other conditions, and are not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Appetite... weight... no, I can't say that I have. No changes there. 

I mean, I know a lot of guys, when they go through the wringer—a divorce, a move, all that stress—they either hit the bottle and blow up like a balloon, or they just stop eating entirely and waste away to nothing. You see it all the time in my line of work. The stress eats at them. But for me... no. My weight has been sitting at a solid 190 pounds since I was about twenty-eight years old, and it hasn't budged an inch, even these past fourteen months. 

I know this for a fact because I wear the exact same size uniform pants I've worn for the last decade. You know the ones—those heavy navy-blue poly-blend trousers with the reinforced knees? The department issues us three new pairs a year, and I always just check the exact same boxes on the quartermaster's requisition form: 34 waist, 32 inseam. They still fit exactly the same. Even my duty belt still fastens on the exact same notch—the third hole from the end. It’s actually got a little wear mark right on that spot from where the brass buckle rubs against the leather every single shift for years. If I was gaining or losing weight, that belt would be the first thing to tell me, because you feel it immediately when you're carrying all that gear around your waist. 

And as for my appetite... it's just the same as it's always been, which is to say, I eat because I have to. It’s exactly like putting gas in the truck. I don't really get cravings for anything, but I haven't stopped eating, either. It’s just... routine. Every Sunday, even now, even when I'm feeling like I'm dragging a hundred-pound anchor around and I can barely get out of that broken recliner I told you about, I force myself to go to the grocery store over on 5th Avenue. The one with the terrible parking lot where people just leave their carts right in the middle of the empty spaces. 

I go in, I buy the exact same things: a loaf of wheat bread, a pound of sliced turkey breast, some apples, a bag of coffee, and those pre-made salads in the plastic clamshells. I come home, I put them in the fridge. And then during the week, I just eat them. I don't really even taste it anymore, to be perfectly honest with you. It's just fuel. I sit in the chair, I eat my turkey sandwich, I throw the paper plate in the trash, and that's it. I'm definitely not eating more, because I don't get any joy out of food right now, no urges to go grab a burger or order a pizza like I used to. And I'm not eating less, because I know if I skip meals, I'll get lightheaded on the job, and I absolutely cannot have that. My squad relies on me to be alert. 

So, no. No changes in the weight, no changes in how much I eat. It's just the exact same maintenance routine, week in and week out, just keeping the engine running even though the car isn't really going anywhere.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has experienced any changes in sleep patterns during the past 14 months—specifically whether he is sleeping more than usual, less than usual, or experiencing difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep.
doctor.question: During these past 14 months, have you noticed any changes in your sleep? For example, are you sleeping more than you normally do, or having trouble falling asleep or staying asleep at night?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in sleep, which is not covered by any of the symptoms in my profile.

patient.answer:
Sleep? No. No, honestly, sleep is about the only thing in my life that hasn't completely flipped upside down on me. 

I mean, you’d think I’d be tossing and turning, right? With everything that’s happened—the divorce, the move to this tiny place, just feeling like I'm dragging that anchor around all day—most guys I know would be up all night staring at the ceiling fan. My ex-wife, actually, she had terrible insomnia whenever she got stressed. She used to get up and pace the hardwood floors in our old house, make this chamomile tea that smelled like wet weeds, and just wander around. Drove me crazy because the floorboards right outside our bedroom door had this awful squeak, and you could hear it all the way down the hall. 

But me? I've never been like that. Even now. I go to bed at 2100 hours, maybe 2130 at the absolute latest, because like I told you, I have to be up at 0500 for my shift. It’s a discipline thing. I bought this cheap, firm mattress from a discount place out on Highway 9 when I first moved into this apartment—the guy tied it to the roof of my truck with twine, if you can believe that, I had to drive twenty miles an hour all the way home—and the second my head hits the pillow, I'm out. Takes me maybe ten minutes to fall asleep. 

And I stay asleep, too. The walls in this complex are paper thin. The people upstairs have this dog, sounds like a beagle mix maybe, that howls, and sometimes it sounds like they’re dropping bowling balls on the floor at two in the morning. But it doesn't wake me up. I sleep right through it, solid as a rock, same as I always have. 

And as for sleeping more... no, I don't do that either. You'd think, given how drained I feel, how I just don't have the energy to participate in anything, that I'd just stay in bed for fourteen hours a day. But my body just doesn't work like that. My eyes snap open at 0455, exactly five minutes before my alarm goes off. It’s this old digital clock I've had since my night-class days, with these glaring red LED numbers that are almost too bright for the room. But I always beat it by five minutes. Even on my days off, I’m awake at 0455. I just get up, make my coffee, and move over to that broken brown recliner. I don't go back to sleep. So, no... falling asleep, staying asleep, how much I sleep... it's all exactly the same routine it's been for the last twenty years. No changes there at all.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced guilt, worthlessness, or self-blame related to the divorce or other circumstances, which would help confirm major depressive disorder and rule out adjustment disorder or other conditions
doctor.question: During these past 14 months, have you found yourself feeling guilty about the divorce, or blaming yourself for how things turned out? Or do you feel like you're worthless or that you've let people down?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of guilt, self-blame, or worthlessness. My symptom profile does not contain an item for guilt or worthlessness.

patient.answer:
Guilty? Worthless? No. No, I wouldn't say that at all. 

I mean, look, the divorce... it was just a thing that happened. It’s like a contract expiring. We were married, and then we just weren't anymore. I remember the exact day we went to the mediator to finalize the division of assets. It was this stuffy little office downtown, right across the street from the municipal courthouse where I have to go testify on cases sometimes. The air conditioning in this guy's office was completely busted, and he just kept wiping his forehead with this yellow handkerchief the whole time we were talking. We sat there, and we divided up the furniture, the savings accounts... I didn't fight her on any of it. She wanted the house, fine. She wanted the good pots and pans, the television, fine. I just packed my duffel bags, grabbed my uniforms, and moved into that cramped apartment I told you about.

But feeling guilty about it? Blaming myself? No. It takes two people to build a marriage, and it takes two people to let it fall apart. We just stopped connecting. The shifts I work—rotating days, nights, weekends, the mandatory overtime—it just grinds you down. You come home and you just want absolute quiet. She wanted to go out, she wanted to talk, and I just... I didn't have the words. But that's just the reality of the job. You ask any guy in my unit, they'll tell you the divorce rate in our line of work is astronomical. It's just a statistic. I don't feel like I failed or let her down. I provided for her, I paid the mortgage on time every single month, I never missed a payment or did her wrong.

And as for feeling worthless... no, I don't get that either. I know exactly what I'm worth. I put on my uniform, I do my job, I keep people safe. I've got a bachelor's degree in criminal justice, I've got commendations in my personnel file. I know I have value. It's just... like I was saying before about the recliner, I just feel heavy and empty. The battery is dead. But I don't sit there beating myself up or thinking I'm a bad person. It's not a pity party. It's just... a blank slate. So, no, no guilt. No feeling worthless. It just is what it is.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any periods of depressed mood or anhedonia lasting at least 2 weeks before the 14-month onset, to help rule out recurrent depression or bipolar disorder and confirm the single major depressive episode dating to the divorce/move.
doctor.question: I want to go back and ask you one more time to be absolutely certain: Looking at your entire life before that move 14 months ago—your childhood, your teenage years, your twenties, your thirties—was there ever even a two-week stretch where you felt down, blue, or sad, or where you lost interest in things you normally cared about?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of depressive episodes (feeling down, blue, sad, or losing interest in things prior to 14 months ago), which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Before the move? No. I can say with absolute certainty, no. 

I mean, you're asking about my whole life, so let's just look at it. Childhood, teenage years... I was always an even-keeled kid. I grew up over in the north end of town, normal house, normal parents. I played baseball—catcher, mostly, because I liked being involved in every single pitch, calling the game from behind the plate. I had this heavy Rawlings leather mitt that I oiled every single Sunday night with this special conditioner my dad bought at the hardware store. I never sat around moping or feeling blue. I wasn't one of those brooding teenagers who locked themselves in their room to listen to sad music. I was just focused. I knew early on I wanted to get into the department, so I kept my nose clean, did the work, and got my bachelor's degree in criminal justice at the state college. 

Then my twenties... well, my twenties were the academy and my rookie years. You don't have time to feel sad in the academy. They run you absolutely ragged. I remember my training officer, Sergeant Miller—this guy had a voice like a gravel crusher, used to make us run the perimeter track at 0400 in the freezing rain if even one guy's boots weren't shined to a mirror finish. But I didn't lose interest in it. I didn't get down about it. I thrived on it. I loved the structure. I was always the first one on the line, ready to go. 

And my thirties? Same thing. Just working the beat, putting my time in, moving up to senior patrol. I was always the guy who took the extra shifts. If someone called out sick on the swing shift, dispatch knew they could call me. I'd put the uniform on, lace up my boots—those heavy black leather tactical boots with the side-zips, you know, they take about a month of solid walking to break in properly, but once you do they fit like a glove—and I'd just go out there and do the job. I liked my life. I liked my routine. I liked going to the firing range on my days off to keep my qualification scores up, I liked grilling on the back patio at the old house with my ex-wife before things got quiet between us. I cared about all of it. 

So, no. Never. There was never a two-week stretch, or even a two-day stretch, where I felt down or blue or lost interest in the things I cared about. My baseline was always just... steady. A perfectly straight line. I was reliable. It wasn't until fourteen months ago, when I packed those duffel bags and ended up in this tiny apartment, sitting in that broken brown recliner, that the battery just completely died on me and this heavy feeling set in. But before that? Not once. Not ever.
